subject: combined-science

items.q: How does the producer at the start of a food chain obtain its biomass?
items.correct: By using photosynthesis to make glucose
items.misconception: By taking in ready-made food from soil
items.why: Everyday language about feeding plants with fertiliser, and the visible fact that roots take up water and mineral ions from soil, make it seem that the plant is taking in food rather than making it. Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth. The producer synthesises molecules: a green plant or alga makes glucose by photosynthesis, and mineral ions from the soil are not a supply of ready-made food.
items.random_wrong: By feeding on other living organisms

items.q: In the food chain lettuce → slug → hedgehog → fox, the hedgehog is:
items.correct: a secondary consumer in the chain
items.misconception: a tertiary consumer in the chain
items.why: The words primary, secondary and tertiary suggest simple counting, and students count every organism in the chain, including the producer, instead of asking what each organism eats. Producers are eaten by primary consumers, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers and then tertiary consumers. The producer is not counted as a consumer, so in this chain the slug is the primary consumer, the hedgehog the secondary consumer and the fox the tertiary consumer.
items.random_wrong: a primary consumer in the chain

items.q: A graph for a stable community shows that each peak in the number of lynx comes about a year after a peak in the number of hares. What does the graph show?
items.correct: Predator numbers peak after prey numbers
items.misconception: Predator numbers peak ahead of prey
items.why: Students read stable as meaning unchanging, and when two curves are drawn on the same axes they are read as one relationship rather than as a delayed response of one population to the other. In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. More prey allows more predators to be supported, so the peak in predator numbers follows the peak in prey numbers; the larger number of predators then reduces the prey numbers again.
items.random_wrong: Predator numbers peak with the prey numbers

items.q: A student places five quadrats at random in a field and counts the daisies in each: 7, 0, 6, 7, 5. What is the mean number of daisies per quadrat?
items.why: All three terms are taught together as types of average and are often asked for in the same question, so students select whichever value is easiest to read off the list instead of carrying out the calculation. The arithmetic mean is the total of the readings divided by the number of readings. The median is the middle value when the readings are put in order and the mode is the most common value; these are different measures and usually give different answers.

items.q: Counts of daisies per quadrat range from 2 to 46. Which scale should the student use on the y-axis when plotting these results?
items.correct: 0 to 50, marked in equal steps of 5
items.why: Students treat the axis as a list of their own results rather than as a continuous number line, so they write their readings up the side in the order they were recorded, and they choose very large ranges because it feels safe to have room for every value. When plotting and drawing appropriate graphs, an appropriate scale for the axes goes up in equal steps of a sensible size, and is chosen so that the range of the data fills most of the available grid rather than being squashed into a corner.

items.q: What is the role of microorganisms in cycling materials through an ecosystem?
items.correct: They return carbon dioxide to the air and ions to the soil
items.misconception: They take in carbon dioxide from the air and ions from the soil
items.why: Photosynthesis is learned as the plant reaction that takes in carbon dioxide, and microorganisms are thought of only as things that make material disappear, so both are treated as one-way users of carbon rather than as respiring organisms. The carbon cycle returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide to be used by plants in photosynthesis. Microorganisms play a key role in cycling materials through an ecosystem by returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil.
items.random_wrong: They remove carbon dioxide and mineral ions from this cycle

items.q: Which statement describes how the water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land?
items.correct: Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated
items.misconception: Rain water soaks into the ground and cannot be reused
items.why: Decay and drainage are seen as things disappearing, and students rarely see the return route, so they picture a one-way journey out of the ecosystem instead of a cycle. All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms. The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas, and water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.
items.random_wrong: Water used up by living organisms is lost from the land

items.q: Does a food chain have to begin with a producer?
items.correct: All food chains begin with a producer which synthesises molecules, usually a green plant or alga.
items.misconception: The words used for organisms in a food chain — producer, primary consumer and so on — are just labels attached loosely to organisms rather than descriptions of what each organism makes or eats, so any organism, even an animal partway along the chain, can be given the wrong label.
items.why: Students meet food chains as a left-to-right sequence and learn the labels by position rather than by what the organism does, so producer becomes a label for first rather than a description of an organism that synthesises its own molecules. All food chains begin with a producer which synthesises molecules. This is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis, so an animal can never be the producer of a chain.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student places quadrats to estimate the abundance of daisies and one quadrat contains no daisies. What should be done with that quadrat?
items.correct: The zero is recorded and included when the arithmetic mean is calculated.
items.misconception: Quadrats containing none of the species do not count, so quadrats should be put down where the plants can be seen and empty quadrats should be left out of the mean.
items.why: A zero looks like a failed reading rather than a result, and students want each quadrat to show them something, so they move the quadrat to a patch of plants or drop the zero when dividing. Quadrats are used to determine the abundance of a species and are placed at random, so a quadrat containing none of the species is a valid result. The arithmetic mean is the total of all the readings divided by the number of quadrats used, including those that contained none.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
